content: Intramuscular injections should be administered in the gluteus maximus or the mid-lateral thigh. For children, it is recommended to use the mid-lateral muscles of the thigh for intramuscular injections. In infants and small children, the upper outer quadrant of the gluteal region should only be used when absolutely necessary, such as in burn patients, to minimize the risk of sciatic nerve injury. The deltoid area should only be used in well-developed individuals, such as certain adults and older children, and even then, with caution to avoid radial nerve injury. Intramuscular injections should not be administered into the lower or mid-third of the upper arm. Aspiration is necessary for all intramuscular injections to avoid accidental injection into a blood vessel. Injection sites should be alternated to prevent complications. When higher doses or prolonged therapy with streptomycin are required for severe or fulminating infections (e.g., endocarditis, meningitis), physicians must take appropriate measures to monitor for any toxic signs or symptoms in the patient. 1. Tuberculosis: The standard treatment regimen for drug-susceptible tuberculosis includes two months of isoniazid (INH), rifampin, and pyrazinamide, followed by four months of INH and rifampin. Patients with concurrent tuberculosis and HIV infection may require longer treatment durations. When streptomycin is added to the regimen due to suspected or confirmed drug resistance, it is typically administered as a single daily intramuscular injection. The total cumulative dose should not exceed 120 grams over the course of therapy unless no other therapeutic options are available. In patients over 60 years of age, the dosage should be reduced due to the increased risk of toxicity. Therapy with streptomycin should be discontinued if toxic symptoms appear, if impending toxicity is suspected, if the organisms become resistant, or if the full therapeutic effect has been achieved. The total duration of tuberculosis treatment is a minimum of one year, but streptomycin therapy may be terminated earlier based on the above indications. 2. Tularemia: Streptomycin is administered at a dose of 1 to 2 grams daily in divided doses for 7 to 14 days, continuing until the patient has been afebrile for 5 to 7 days. 3. Plague: Streptomycin is administered intramuscularly at a dose of 2 grams daily in two divided doses. A minimum of 10 days of therapy is recommended. 4. Bacterial Endocarditis: For bacterial endocarditis caused by organisms with low streptomycin minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs), streptomycin may be used for a two-week treatment course in combination with penicillin. If ototoxicity occurs, streptomycin therapy may need to be discontinued before completing the six-week treatment course. 5. Concomitant Use with Other Agents: Streptomycin is considered a second-line agent for treating gram-negative bacillary bacteremia, meningitis, pneumonia, brucellosis, granuloma inguinale, chancroid, and urinary tract infections when used in combination with other agents to which the infecting organism is sensitive. For adults: The recommended dose is 1 to 2 grams daily in divided doses every 6 to 12 hours for moderate to severe infections. Doses should generally not exceed 2 grams per day. For children: The recommended dose is 20 to 40 mg/kg/day (8 to 20 mg/lb/day) in divided doses every 6 to 12 hours. Care must be taken to avoid excessive dosing in children. The dry lyophilized streptomycin cake should be reconstituted by adding Water for Injection USP to achieve the desired concentration. The sterile reconstituted solution should be protected from light and can be stored at room temperature for up to one week without significant loss of potency. Parenteral drug products should be visually inspected for particulate matter and discoloration prior to administration, whenever the solution and container permit.
